en: The Mahāmāyā Sūtra, Scroll One; also titled *The Buddha Ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanjing of the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in the Pārijāta tree grove within the Nandana Garden in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

He observed the three-month rains retreat beneath a *citrā* tree, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, surrounded before and behind by countless other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
At that time, the Tathāgata sat in the full lotus posture, emitting a thousand rays of light from the pores of his body, which universally illuminated the trichiliocosm.
Within each ray of light were a thousand lotuses, and upon each lotus sat a thousand transformation Buddhas in the full lotus posture, identical to Śākyamuni.

At that time, the majestic radiance of the sun, moon, and stars was eclipsed and no longer appeared; they all entered into the light of the Tathāgata, causing the pārijātaka tree to appear like the color of pure gold.
Just as the sky is pure and free from clouds and mists, so that the majestic radiance of the sun and moon is extremely clear and manifest;
even so is the light emitted by the Tathāgata while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, shining with a brilliance many times greater than before, beyond all comparison.

At that time, the sons of gods of the sun, moon, and stars, having seen these signs, their hearts were struck with trembling and fear such that they could not find peace; they did not know for what cause such a thing had occurred.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Go to your mother and tell her that I am here; I wish for her to deign to pay homage to the Triple Gem for a moment, and speak these verses to her."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Great Seer Śākyamuni, who has accomplished all-knowledge,
dwells here in Jambudvīpa, like the Thousand-Eyed Deva."
With earnest longing and ardent yearning, I have long desired to behold your compassionate countenance.
Formerly, within the royal palace, seven days after my birth, my spirit ascended to receive celestial blessings; my maternal aunt then nurtured me with her milk.
Having attained perfect enlightenment, I am now an Arhat who delivers sentient beings.
I have come here for this very purpose: to preach the Dharma and repay my past kindness.
I pray that you, Mother, together with your retinue, will deign to come to this place.
"I pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and I shall receive the true and pure Dharma.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having received the Buddha’s command, immediately went to where Mahāmāyā was and reported the Buddha’s words in full, reciting the verses spoken by the Tathāgata.
When Mahāmāyā heard these words, milk flowed forth from her breasts spontaneously, and she spoke thus:
"If it is certain that this is Siddhārtha born of me, let this milk flow directly into his mouth."
Having spoken these words, milk issued from both her breasts—resembling white lotuses—and entered the mouth of the Tathāgata.

When Mahāmāyā beheld this, her entire body leaped with joy and her countenance became serene and radiant, like a thousand-petaled lotus blooming under the sun; Mahāmāyā’s exquisite beauty was likewise transformed. At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook everywhere, and various wonderful flowers and fruits blossomed and ripened out of season. She then addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Since I have been the mother of the Buddha, I have never experienced such joy and peace as I do now."
Just as someone suffering from extreme hunger and thirst might suddenly encounter a sumptuous feast and partake of it with great joy;
so too is my present delight, such that no other miscellaneous or distracted thoughts remain.
Having spoken these words, she immediately set out for the Buddha’s dwelling together with the youth Mañjuśrī.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw his mother approaching from afar; inwardly filled with joy and reverence, his entire body vibrated with a movement like that of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and the four great oceans being stirred.
At that time, when the Tathāgata saw that his mother had arrived, he addressed her in a Brahma-voice, saying:
"The body, wherever it goes, is accompanied by suffering and pleasure; you should cultivate nirvāṇa to forever leave behind both suffering and pleasure."

At that time, Mahāmāyā, having heard these words of the Buddha, joined her palms and bowed her head, contemplating with single-minded focus. She knelt before the Buddha and prostrated herself, fully applying right mindfulness so that all her fetters were subdued and extinguished.
Then, before the Buddha, he praised him with these verses:
"From incalculable eons past, you have constantly drunk my breast milk;
Therefore, having transcended birth, old age, and death, you have attained the Unsurpassed Way."
One ought to repay his grace and nourishment by severing the root of my three poisons.
I take refuge in the Great Man, who is free from greed and practices generous giving;
I take refuge in the Tamer of Men, the supreme one whom none can surpass.
I take refuge in the Teacher of Gods and Humans, who is forever free from the bonds of delusion and craving.
Three times each day and night, with unceasing mindfulness,
I bow my head to the ground in prostration before the Unsurpassed Great Dharma King.
Now, within this field of merit that you are, I wish to nurture the sprouts of virtue;
I pray only that you bestow compassion and swiftly cause these to ripen into wondrous fruit.
Having long harbored this great aspiration, I was thus born into the palace of a great king.
"With a massive body of purple-gold color, his radiance illuminates the ten directions;
his countenance is perfectly round and pure, like the full moon in autumn.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed his mother, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.

It is good in the beginning, middle, and end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching; its phrasing is exquisite, pure, and unadulterated; it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life."
Upon hearing these words, Mahāmāyā—through the supernatural power of the Buddha and because her roots of goodness had reached full maturity—immediately recognized her past lives;
she severed eighty billion bonds of smoke and flame and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
He immediately rose, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have already realized liberation from the prison of birth and death.
When the great assembly gathered there heard these words, they spoke with one voice, saying:
"May all sentient beings attain liberation, just as Mahāmāyā does now.
Then Mahāmāyā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is like a fierce fire burning hot iron; if anyone touches it, their body and mind will be scorched with pain."
The cycle of birth and death in this world is likewise so; every place to which one comes and goes is a mass of suffering.

The root of all accumulated suffering lies in the mind, which, following its desires, is flighty and frivolous, playing with sentient beings as they revolve through the five realms faster than a fierce wind, like a bouncing ball.
Then Mahāmāyā, before the Buddha, reproached her own mind, saying: "Why do you constantly act against my benefit?
You wander through the realms of the six sense-objects without stability; pulled by distracted thoughts, you never pause for a moment."
All objects of perception are devoid of auspiciousness; for what reason do you delude me and cause me to gather them?
It is like a person who constantly tills the earth—the great earth itself is never diminished or increased by this, yet his farming tools wear away daily.
It is likewise in the ocean of birth and death: though one constantly discards body and life beyond measure, my consciousness remains fundamentally neither increasing nor decreasing.
"You were able to cause me to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four quarters of the world with the seven treasures complete;
yet in an instant you caused me to fall back and become a frog,
and in another instant you caused me to become a poor and lowly man, running hither and thither in search of food and clothing."
In one moment, you cause me to become a great wealthy householder, with riches accumulated in the hundreds of millions and my fame heard everywhere;
in another moment, you cause me to dwell in celestial palaces, partaking of ambrosia and indulging at will in the five desires;
and in yet another moment, you cause me to reside in hell, drinking molten copper and swallowing glowing iron balls.
I have merely, in the past, possessed the bodies of oxen; were their hides piled together, they would reach as high as Mount Sumeru, yet I still had not attained liberation from birth and death.
In an instant, I again acquired immeasurable names:

sometimes called a master, sometimes a servant, sometimes a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), sometimes a monarch, or a deva, nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, asura, garuḍa, kiṃnara, mahoraga, human, or non-human; or called an animal, a hungry ghost (preta), or a hell-being—sentient beings have such various designations as these.

"O deluded mind, although you have previously possessed the five worldly desires—gold, silver, various treasures, wife and children, male and female slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, houses, fields and dwellings, people, and villages—all these have soon dispersed and vanished, joining together in impermanence."
That which is temporarily regarded as one's own will ultimately return to destruction, like a guesthouse where no single host remains for long.

Even those who reach the heavens and possess mastery over the five desires, when their merit is exhausted and they approach the end of life, the five signs of decay appear; they then wander about in longing and attachment, their hearts filled with sorrow and suffering.
Furthermore, among human beings, they are impoverished and lowly, driven into service by others;
or if they occupy royal thrones, they engage in mutual warfare, with rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, vying with one another to destroy each other.
Descending as far as the hells, they are slaughtered, dismembered, burned, and boiled;
among the animals, they prey upon one another, devouring skin, flesh, sinews, and strength to repay their past debts, constrained by their karma and lacking any autonomy;
among the hungry ghosts, driven by hunger and thirst, they run hither and thither, seeing only masses of fire and glowing iron wheels constantly following behind them.
Within the cycle of birth and death across the five realms of existence, there are such various sufferings as these, beyond measure or calculation.
"O deluded mind, from time immemorial you have long led me to wander through all places of coming and going, always following me in compliance, never once acting in opposition."

Today I wish to listen exclusively to the Dharma; do not again cause disturbance or create obstacles. You, too, should cultivate weary detachment from all suffering and swiftly seek nirvana to quickly attain peace and happiness.
Then Mahāmāyā spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“May you pour down the rain of Dharma, To moisten and nourish all that is withered;
May the sprouts of Dharma grow everywhere, Blossoming and gradually flourishing.”
May I and this assembly have our roots of goodness fully ripened;
may we each attain the fruits of the various paths in due order.
I pray that you bestow the nectar of the Dharma at this time, to extinguish the very source of greed and hatred.
We have wandered through the long night, bound and fettered within the prison of ignorance;
bewildered and lacking wisdom, we did not know where to seek the Way.
We pray that you will show us the path to liberation, so that we may swiftly reach the city of eternal bliss.
At that time, after Mahāmāyā had spoken these verses, she again praised the Buddha in verse before him:
“The World-Honored One stands amidst the great assembly, His radiance surpassing Mount Sumeru.
I now bow my head in prostration To the Buddha, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha.”
The fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, with parched longing and earnest devotion,
gaze upon the Buddha with single-minded attention as if with unblinking celestial eyes;
they yearn only for their Ornamented Teacher to be adorned with the garland of the sublime Dharma.
At that time, having spoken these verses of praise, Mahāmāyā addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I truly know that the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as kings, ministers, elders, householders, and brahmins—is immeasurable in number; and the verses of praise and hymns they have spoken extolling the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous merits are likewise immeasurable."

"Yet now, my wisdom is but slight and shallow, and I still desire to offer even a small portion of praise for the great ocean of the Buddha’s merits; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
He then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"The mountain of wisdom is lofty and vast, Its peaks and ridges are most formidable."
The mountain streams and valleys are deep and vast, where clear springs flow perpetually full.
Various medicinal herbs for curing ailments grow luxuriantly by their side;
should anyone partake of them, they shall enjoy eternal and boundless bliss.
Just as the sugarcane seed, Its inner nature is always sweet;
When the wise press it well, They obtain a delicious flavor.
The Dharma taught by the World-Honored One Is pure from its very origin.
If a person has faith and joy in receiving [the Dharma], their meritorious retribution will be inexhaustible.
Although all sentient beings have boundless aspirations and desires,
only the Honored Muni can bring them all to fulfillment.
The afflictions of sentient beings have burned fiercely from time immemorial;
The Tathāgata, the Great King of Physicians, administers wholesome medicine according to the ailment.
The crooked paths of birth and death are perilous and difficult to traverse.
The five, including Kauṇḍinya, wandered on without knowing how to return.
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata went in person to Vārāṇasī;
for their sake he turned the Wheel of Dharma, and they all attained the realization of the fruits of the Path.
Eighty thousand sons of heaven attained the Dharma-eye in mid-air;
were it not for the Great Teacher, who else could have turned them back?
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and Kātyāyana—
These four great śrāvakas, before they had left the household life, were of lofty talent and broad learning; yet they were arrogant and looked down upon the world.
All the nation revered them, and no one could equal their fame and virtue.
Upon hearing the nectar of the Dharma but once, he subdued his passions and became an Arhat;
gradually assisting the Great Master, he followed in accordance with him as the Wheel of Dharma was turned.
Like the nyagrodha tree, its seed is exceedingly minute, yet it grows into a great banyan.
Lush and flourishing as it grows with the seasons, its branches and twigs hang down far and wide;
so too is the progress of those transformed and delivered by the World-Honored One.
Like Aṅgulimāla, who had killed many sentient beings—
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, transformed him and caused him to enter the Buddha-way.
That Devadatta committed five acts of immediate retribution;
he commanded spirits to lift a great boulder, intending to harm the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One regards all with equanimity, as if they were Rāhula.
Furthermore, that Mother of Ghosts, who constantly devours human children,
hid her own son so he would not appear, out of the Buddha’s compassion.
Terrified and frantic, they searched everywhere, unable to know where he was;
returning, they questioned the World-Honored One, seeking to be shown his son’s whereabouts.
The Tathāgata, through skillful means, immediately questioned them regarding the matter at hand:
"Because you yourself cherish your own child, you run about in haste to seek it out.
How can you lack a heart of compassion and constantly devour the children of others?
Take yourself as an analogy for others: do not kill, do not wield the rod."
"If you can transform this mind, you shall see your son now.
Having heard these words, she felt both shame and joy;
bowing her head in prostration, she also spoke to the Buddha with palms joined on behalf of her son:
"From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall abandon the mind of greed and harm.
Having thus received the five precepts, he proceeded until he attained the fruits of the Path.
Just as that Mother of Ghosts, out of love for her own child,
extended [her compassion] to others at large and ultimately and forever renounced killing;
may the World-Honored One of Great Compassion likewise do so now.
"Out of compassion for my mother who gave birth to me, and extending it to all others,
I pray that you will swiftly open the gates of the True Dharma, so that all beings may hear and receive it.
At that time, after Mahāmāyā had spoken this verse, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings within the five realms of existence are brought about by the faults and afflictions of defilements; therefore, they are bound by fetters and lack self-mastery.”
"I vow that when I attain perfect enlightenment in a future life, I shall sever the very root of all these afflictions.

It is only our Great Teacher who compassionately regards the world, seeing how birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, and suffering—the fire of impermanence—constantly burn sentient beings, blazing through the long night without ever ceasing. He calls his disciples to return to his abode, revealing the perilous root of birth and death, and says to them:

'Why do you sleep so long upon the bed of the triple-world’s wheel of fire? The demon of impermanent death watches for an opening to seize you; the various diseases and the blades of the wind-sickness seek to cut short human life.'"

For example, when thieves see a treasury of precious jewels, they take up weapons and come to attack; for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas they undergo various other forms, and only by practicing the ten wholesome deeds do they finally obtain a human body.

Though having obtained a human body, long life is likewise difficult to find; yet the evil thief of impermanence further inflicts oppression, so one ought to be cautious and vigilant, yet still remains self-indulgent.

"Foolish people vainly calculate the number of days, months, and years, deeming them fixed periods; they fail to perceive that every thought-moment shifts and passes away in secret. When their lives finally end, they are reborn according to their karma, while their households and kinsmen weep together in mutual grief—this cycle continues thus without end."
"Human beings in this world are like flashes of lightning; yet within this very state, they give rise to arrogance, some even declaring:
'I am a king who rules over the world, possessing sovereign power and authority.'"
Some may declare:
"I am a great minister who assists in the affairs of state; whether a matter is unjust or upright depends on me.
Others may declare:
"I am a wealthy elder, possessing abundant riches and treasures; whatever I desire is at my command.
Or some may declare:
"I am of the Brahmin caste, of noble lineage, intelligent and widely learned; my ancestors have successively served as teachers to the Kṣatriyas."
"World-Honored One!
While these people were in the world, they enjoyed all manner of pleasures at their own will and ease, never having any anxiety or concern;
yet once death arrives, they harbor regret and remorse—what can they do then?"
"When one is in the prime of strength, one follows along with kinsmen, indulging in play and dissipation, failing to cultivate even the slightest merit;
yet when impermanence suddenly arrives, each is scattered to one of the five destinies, and for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, it will be difficult to encounter one another again."

Birth and death are without reality, like a city of the gandharvas. Even those such as the pratyekabuddhas, who have exhausted all fetters and outflows and possess great supernormal powers—moving with sovereign fearlessness, emitting fire from the upper body and water from the lower body, or emitting water from the upper body and fire from the lower body; flying through the air, moving, standing, sitting, lying down, coming and going with such swiftness that stone walls offer no obstruction; possessing upright features and endowed with all the marks, able to serve as a great field of merit for sentient beings—even they cannot yet escape the affliction of impermanence, just as one might use a great flood of water to extinguish a small fire.
When people of the world violate the laws of the king and their crime merits death, such that they are confined in prison, they may still be saved through intercession and thus obtain release;
however, the law of impermanence cannot be interceded for.
"If even those with the power of the noble sages cannot escape this, how much less can ordinary people be free from sorrow and fear?

There was a seer of the five supernormal powers named Daivayāna; another seer named Udraka Rāmaputra; another named Viśvāmitra; another named Ārāḍa; another named Parāśara; another named Aṅgiras; another named Asita; and another named Vasiṣṭha. Such great seers as these were endowed with majestic power and possessed great renown; they could, by means of incantations and arts, bring cities and towns to prosperity or ruin. Where are these individuals now?"
"Because the fire of impermanence has once burned sentient beings, it now turns back to consume itself, leading all to extinction.

Great Brahmā Deva King, Śakra Devendra, Maheśvara, the Māra Kings of the six heavens of desire, Viṣṇu, and Yama Rāja—along with the spirits Rāvaṇa, Rāvaṇi, Piśāci, Garuḍi, and Varuṇi—all these of great power have been seized by impermanence."

“King Mūrdhaja, King Nārāyaṇa, King Cīccharāja, King Aśvaghoṣa, and King Vinirāśi—these kings ruled over many nations; they were handsome in appearance, possessed world-surpassing intelligence, and their physical strength was so courageous and robust that none could withstand them. Yet, crushed by impermanence, one knows not where they have gone.”

“Sāgara, the Dragon King; Śūdrīśana, the Ghost King; Vemacitrin, the Asura King; and the celestial queens Śacī, Mṛṇālā, Utpalā, Tiṣyā, Aghalā, Ālūpā, Mādrī, and Mādrīśā—these various kings possessed great majesty and power, and their many queens were of peerless beauty. Should anyone behold them, they would immediately lose right mindfulness; their minds would become distracted by perverse thoughts as if possessed by non-human spirits, such that even the most skilled physicians could not cure them through various treatments to restore their right mindfulness. Yet even these have all returned to impermanence.”

"Just as a hunter surrounds and pursues various beasts, so too is the law of impermanence: it drives and presses sentient beings toward the abode of King Yama, causing the elephants of karma to trample them one after another; the tigers of impermanence constantly lie in wait for sentient beings, and whenever they find an opportunity, they devour them together."
Just as when a caṇḍāla wishes to slaughter a sheep, he hangs its two feet upside down so that it cannot leap about;
the caṇḍāla of impermanence is likewise, seizing all sentient beings so that they cannot move or turn.
The law of impermanence is like the *aja-kara* snake, which, upon seeing a person, coils its two heads around them;
the law of impermanence is like a banner in the wind, which topples over at the very moment it has gathered;
the law of impermanence is also like the dark fortnight of the moon, gradually waning until it turns toward total obscurity.
When Mahāmāyā had spoken these words, she further recited in verse:
"Just as a *caṇḍāla* drives an ox toward the slaughterhouse,
With every step drawing closer to the ground of death, The life of a human being passes even more swiftly than this."
When Mahāmāyā had spoken these verses, she addressed the great assembly gathered before the Buddha, saying:
"O brothers and sisters among all dharmas, you should diligently cultivate the practice of the precepts."
Now, fortunately, you have encountered the Unsurpassed Teacher, who holds the torch of Dharma to illuminate the practitioner and provides clothing and provisions so that nothing is lacking.
If you wish to reach the City of Peace and Bliss, you should quickly consult him regarding the path that leads correctly.

If there are those who encounter such a virtuous guide yet do not take refuge in them or follow their instructions, one should know that such persons are extremely stubborn and will certainly commit the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution.

The ocean of suffering of birth and death is truly terrifying. Within a single kalpa, the various bodies one has undergone have accumulated skin that would equal Mount Sumeru; the times spent sleeping and lying within the womb, the countless entries and exits through the foul-smelling secretions, as well as the milk-fed stages involving excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva, and even the immeasurable sufferings of old age and death—let alone the agonizing torments of the three miserable realms.
"Therefore, I now address you all: exert yourselves throughout the long night to seek liberation.
At that time, Mahāmāyā rose from her seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Why is it that all sentient beings sink and wallow within birth and death, unable to know the path of transcendence?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Mahāmāyā:

"The reason sentient beings do not attain liberation is entirely due to greed, hatred, and delusion. For this reason, they remain perpetually within birth and death; even the desire to seek rebirth in heaven is difficult to achieve, let alone the hope of departing from birth and death."
While in this world, one also loses a good reputation; friends and relatives all abandon one, regarding one as mere grass or soil, no longer feeling any affection.
At the moment of death, one experiences extreme terror and, with a bewildered consciousness, only then feels regret and self-reproach—all of which arises from the afflictions of the three poisons.
"If a person desires to seek the sublime fruit of liberation, they should sever the root of suffering.
Those foolish worldlings are bound by fetters, just as a wicked horse, tethered by its halter and bit, cannot move."

That is to say, one does not know as they truly are the arising of form, the cessation of form, and attachment to form; nor does one know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are. Consequently, one does not attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.

If one can attain liberation regarding form and know it as it truly is to its ultimate extent, then one will likewise know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are to their ultimate extent, thereby attaining liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress; this is called severing the root of suffering.
Once the root of suffering has been severed, one is free from delusive conceptualization;

being free from delusive conceptualization, one is without攀缘 (pāra-ālambana, objective clinging), and no longer craves or adheres to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, thereby abandoning attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.
"From this day forward, you should mutually reveal and teach this Dharma to one another, so that you may long obtain benefit.
You should now listen to what I say.

Throughout incalculable kalpas in the past, I have extensively practiced asceticism for the sake of all sentient beings, thereby attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. My compassion for all is like that for an only child, and the conditions for those who should be transformed and delivered are now nearing their completion."
The Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is that of the Sugata; there is no further occasion for them to return to the world.

Once I have passed away from here, my traces will be difficult to find. I shall not return to become a lord of Jambudvīpa, nor shall I become a lord of Aparagoyānī, nor a lord of Pūrvavideha, nor a lord of Uttarakuru. I shall not become a Cakravartin King, nor Śakra Devānām Indra, nor Mahābrahmā.

Having thus completely renounced the three realms, I have long since established myself securely as a sovereign Dharma King. I do not subdue the people with swords, weapons, fetters, or shackles, but rather bestow the True Dharma upon sentient beings, causing all to attain liberation.
Meeting must inevitably lead to separation; such is the nature of the power of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Even the precious Mount Sumeru will be consumed and destroyed at the end of an eon, and the four great oceans will likewise dry up. When a Tathāgata appears in the world to deliver sentient beings, he cannot remain once the conditions for his work are exhausted.
"Impermanence is as vile and evil as a large tortoise or crocodile; once it bites a person, it never lets go.
When the great assembly gathered there heard these words, they wailed in grief and were filled with distress, speaking together in a single voice with this verse:
"The Buddha-sun has appeared in the world, Its radiance shining with eternal brilliance."
Now I wish to remain hidden, entering the mountain of impermanence.
O Guide! God among Gods!
O Peerless and Supreme Being!
How is it that those beings are being plundered by the thieves of conditioned existence?
Those of meager merit find themselves in the long night of utter darkness.

At that time, the World-Honored One had been preaching various teachings for the sake of the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven until the end of the third month, intending to return down to Jambudvīpa.
Even if one were to command the son of a great minister in the city of Rājagṛha—named Kumāra, who was clever, eloquent, and wise—and say to him:

"You should now descend to Jambudvīpa and travel throughout all the kingdoms, making it universally known that the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa, and proclaim this extensively by means of these verses."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The entire world is now blind and dark, Having lost the eye of wisdom;
The roots of the three poisons grow ever deeper, Because there is no King of Physicians.”
Furthermore, he intends to depart for that city of Nirvana, deep and remote.
Now residing in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he preaches the Dharma to transform sentient beings;
you virtuous ones should quickly invite him to descend again to Jambudvīpa.

Then Kumāra, having received the Buddha’s command, descended to Jambudvīpa and traveled throughout all the kingdoms, proclaiming it everywhere and reciting the verses bestowed upon him by the Tathāgata.
At that time, having heard the words spoken by Kumāra, the sentient beings were overcome with extreme grief and distress. They all bowed their heads at his feet and spoke thus:

"For some time now we have been deprived of the compassionate protection [of our teacher], and the poisonous fires of the world have grown ever more fierce. We all did not know where the Great Master was; it is now revealed that he is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and furthermore, he intends before long to enter parinirvāṇa."
How bitter it is that the Eye of the World is about to perish!
Our sinful bodies are utterly separated from those of devas and humans, leaving us with no means to ascend to heaven to pay our respects and offer our entreaties.
We only pray that you, O Benevolent One, out of universal compassion for us, will return to the heavens and address the Buddha on our behalf, saying:

"All sentient beings within Jambudvīpa prostrate together from afar at the feet of the World-Honored One. Having long been separated from your holy transformation, there are none who do not look up with longing and yearning. We have searched in all four directions but did not know where you were; only now do we hear that you are in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, bringing vast benefit to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, we hear that before long you shall enter parinirvāṇa, and the world will then lose its eye of wisdom."
"I only pray that you will take pity on the people of Jambudvīpa and quickly descend once more to bestow upon them the medicine of the Dharma.
When Kumārajīva heard these words, he immediately ascended to heaven again, went to where the Buddha was, and related to the Buddha in full detail everything the people of Jambudvīpa had said.
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One emitted five-colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and crystal-red—and these lights shone everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the people—men, women, great and small—seeing this radiance, were all filled with wonder and joy; they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to one another:
"What sudden cause for such a strange omen as this?"
This is not the light of the sun, moon, or stars, nor can it be produced by the supernatural powers, spells, or incantations of the five-fold transcendent sages (pañcābhijña-ṛṣi) or the brahmins.
Furthermore, some said:

"As we observe this radiance now, it is certainly not the work of any other power; it must be that the Greatly Compassionate, Unsurpassed King of Physicians has emitted this auspicious sign out of pity for the world, so that we might perhaps receive peace and relief."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that the Buddha was about to descend, immediately commanded the spirits and deities to construct three jeweled stairways—using Jāmbūnada gold for the central stairway, pure lapis lazuli for the stairway on the right side, and pure agate for the stairway on the left side—the balustrades and carvings of which were exceedingly magnificent and beautiful.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmāyā, saying:
"The law of birth and death is such that meeting must inevitably end in separation.
I should now descend and return to Jambudvīpa; before long, I too shall enter into parinirvāṇa."
When Mahāmāyā heard these words, she shed tears and spoke this verse:
"Because the World-Honored One, throughout vast eons, Out of compassion for all beings,
Gave up his head, eyes, marrow, and brain, He has now attained Perfect Enlightenment."
"All sentient beings within the three realms are long lost in the ocean of ignorance and craving;
it is precisely for them that you should provide the boat of Dharma. Why then do you turn your back and abandon them?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is not without cause.
When conditions are exhausted, how could they remain?
Such is the nature of the Buddha-dharma throughout the three periods of time.”

At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One, desiring to repay the kindness of her who gave birth to him and out of compassion for all sentient beings, spoke this mantra before Mahāmāyā:
“Namo buddhāya, namo dharmāya.”
Namo saṃghāya, namo sātatyasamyaksaṃbuddhaśrāvakasaṃghāya,
namo maitreyaparamokṣāya.
Homage to the Stream-enterers;
homage to the Once-returners; homage to the Non-returners;
homage to the Arhats.
Namo lokasamyak-kathana-samyak-paripūrṇa-nayati-samagra-hita-phala-vyakta-mahā-mayūri-vijara-jarā-bhaya-śamani-śeṣa-tri-śeṣate.
Mukhendu-mi-ji-kṣu-pāra-devī-vicari-carā-caradeva-nāga-yakṣa-asura-garuḍa-kinnara-mahoraga-yakṣa-rākṣasa-viśvaca-sigandha-umā-simhala-ka-mukhendu-mi-buddha-gana-ji-pāra.

Devicchara-cchara-kalpa-ahara-luti-ti-da-ahara-man-ca-ahara-mi-da-ahara-sarva-ahara-atuccha-ahara-gi-vi-da-ahara-ṭha-ciṭṭha-pava-ciṭṭha-kubi-da-ciṭṭha-gaṇḍa-gaṇḍa-na-ciṭṭha-buddha-va-dharma-va-saṃgha-pava-ra-senaka-ku-ṭi-ka-pan-ṭi-kau-pan-ṭi-śrī-ni-yama-rakṣa-yama-thuti.
Lamba palamba kārapaśe ālīte alike ālīte alibhigale lambā vilambā kārapaśe ālīte.
"I now speak this mantra to repay the kindness of my mother who gave me birth, and for the protection of all beings."

If there are good men or good women who, with a sincere heart, desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite what was spoken by Lady Mahāmāyā as well as this mantra, they should first bathe themselves clean and put on fresh, pure clothes. They should smear the ground with fragrant mud, burn incense and powdered incense, scatter various wonderful flowers, and offer various kinds of worship such as silk canopies, banners, and streamers, accompanied by singing and instrumental music. For seven days and seven nights, they should observe the eightfold precepts—abstaining from the five pungent roots, all impure flavors, and the ten kinds of meat, eating none of them at all—and with palms joined in reverence, take refuge in the Triple Gem while reciting the name of Mahāmāyā and chanting this mantra.

By the power of this mantra, one is able to eliminate for sentient beings fevers, malaria, insanity, consumption, possession by malevolent spirits, curses and incantations, seeing evil omens while sleeping, frequent nightmares, somnambulism, dropsy, shortness of breath, as well as infantile convulsions, crying fits, and the afflictions of *chi-mei* and *wang-liang* ghosts; all four hundred and four diseases can be eradicated. Furthermore, one will gain a good reputation in the world and will always be relied upon by all.

"Those who uphold this mantra should also invoke the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka of the South, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa of the West, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa of the North;
as well as the foremost minister of the Eastern Heavenly King named Maṇibhadra, the second named Pūrṇabhadra, and the third named Kumbhīra, who govern all the various ghosts and spirits;

and the foremost ministers of the Southern Heavenly King named Pañcāla, Indrāyudha, Cāmara, and Kharaskandha, each leading five hundred million ghosts and spirits to protect the land of China—'China' being the name for the Han nation—and Jambudvīpa, so that no ghosts may act in disorder."
The six brothers, including Baddhana and others, are the foremost ministers of the Heavenly King of the West;

and the yakṣa Kāpila, the Great Deity Golden-Haired, the Great Deity Thumb-Sized, and the deity Vajrapāṇi (Saṃjñeya) are the foremost ministers of the Heavenly King of the North. Such great spirits and deities as these govern the four continents.

If there are those who read and recite what Mahāmāyā has expounded as well as this divine mantra, these benevolent deities, hearing their names being invoked, will all come to attend upon them, providing protection and service; thus, all afflictions shall be completely extinguished.
At that time, having spoken this mantra, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If there are evil sentient beings who do not comply with this mantra,
they will be like merchants who drift and drown in the land of the rākṣasīs."
Five hundred rākṣasas will vie with one another to seize and devour him;
yet if a person skillfully recites and upholds such a divine mantra,
they will be like merchants who return safely from the great ocean.
One obtains many rare treasures, inexhaustible for seven generations.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have given away my head, eyes, marrow, brain, bones, flesh,
as well as my hands, feet, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children.
Accumulating the bodhisattva practices, Diligently cultivating the pāramitās;
Out of vast compassion for all beings, And not for the sake of one's own body,
One attains perfect enlightenment To rescue and deliver suffering sentient beings.
"By reciting this dhāraṇī, one shall protect the world.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One took his leave of his mother and descended by the jeweled staircase.

Mahābrahmā followed behind holding a parasol, while Śakra-devendra and the Four Heavenly Kings stood in attendance at his left and right. Immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, along with bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, and various other miscellaneous spirits and deities, surrounded him before and behind, filling the void of space. They performed various musical performances, chanted hymns, and offered praises; they burned many kinds of famous incense and scattered various exquisite flowers, leading the way as he descended toward Jambudvīpa.

At that time, the various kings of Jambudvīpa—King Prasenajit, King Udayana, King Bimbisāra, King Mūrdhaga, King Puṣkarasārin, and all other kings—as well as their ministers, elders, householders, and brahmins, each arrayed the fourfold army of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. Adorned in blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated colors, they shone like the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven when they go forth for a tour of inspection.
Together with other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, they gathered at the jeweled stairs to welcome the Buddha.

At that time, King Prasenajit, the ruler of Śrāvastī, immediately commanded his ministers to further prepare various kinds of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions at Jetavana; he ordered that whatever was required be provided and prepared.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had arrived in Jambudvīpa, the kings, ministers, elders, lay devotees, and the fourfold assembly paid him respectful homage, offering songs of praise and eulogies, as they followed the World-Honored One into the Jetavana Monastery.

At that time, when all the people heard that the Tathāgata had returned from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the Jetavana, they all rushed forward in competition, filling and blocking the roads; the four gates of the Jetavana Vihāra were overflowing, and the multitude of those coming and going was beyond calculation.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne, surrounded before and behind by the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.
When King Prasenajit saw the World-Honored One on the lion throne, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"We now take refuge in the one who is a mass of unsurpassed merit."
Skillfully uprooting the source of all suffering, Able to plant the manifold roots of goodness,
Compassionately bestowing blessings upon sentient beings— He is the most supreme Tamer of Men;
With features and marks of such dignified countenance, The body of a peerless Great Being.
The Teacher is a field of merit most excellent, His virtues surpass those of Brahmā and Śakra;
In debate he widely subdues all opponents, And through his spiritual powers he attains mastery.
I now prostrate with my head at the feet Of the peerless Teacher of gods and humans.
When King Prasenajit had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Now sentient beings are submerged in birth and death; drinking poisonous medicine, none can provide a cure. I only pray that the Great Seer will bestow the nectar of immortality upon us."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
“You should know the fundamental source of all birth and death: ignorance conditions volitional formations;

volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.”

If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; if volitional formations cease, then consciousness ceases; if consciousness ceases, then name-and-form ceases; if name-and-form ceases, then the six sense bases cease; if the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases; if contact ceases, then feeling ceases; if feeling ceases, then craving ceases; if craving ceases, then clinging ceases; if clinging ceases, then becoming ceases; if becoming ceases, then birth ceases; if birth ceases, then aging and death cease; and if aging and death cease, then sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
You should all diligently practice with perseverance so that you may swiftly escape the ocean of suffering within the triple world.
Listen further!

Within the phenomena of birth and death, one is constantly bound by the eight sufferings; this is entirely due to the uninterrupted accumulation and circulation of the karmas of body, speech, and mind.
If one can sever the root of all origins (*samudaya*), then all sufferings will cease; one shall practice the Eightfold Noble Path, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and correct way.
If one can examine and contemplate with such discernment, then one may emerge from the boundaries of all states of existence (*bhava*).
The Mahāmāyā Sūtra, Volume One;
The Mahāmāyā Sūtra, Volume Two, also titled *The Buddha Ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanying of the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had preached the sublime Dharma for King Prasenajit and the great assembly,

he was surrounded by the community of bhikṣus as they proceeded from Śrāvastī, traveling gradually through villages and market towns— completing his ministry to all those who were ready to be saved— until he eventually arrived at the Nairañjanā River.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had reached the river, he put on his bathing robe and entered the water to bathe.

Then, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, seeing the Tathāgata bathing in the river, each brought various kinds of ointments and powdered incense to present as offerings.

At that time, on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, among all beings in the water, on land, and in the air, the body of the Tathāgata appeared like a bright mirror. Beholding his wondrous form, they all gave rise to joy and developed hearts of loving-kindness; their three poisons were subdued and extinguished so that they no longer preyed upon one another, and they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, all these sentient beings among the waters, on land, and in the void, having beheld the Buddha’s body, have already given rise to joy and resolved their minds upon Bodhi."

Devadatta was born into the Śākya palace as a kinsman of the Buddha; he became a śramaṇa and constantly recited profound and wondrous sūtras. Yet, he perpetually committed acts of rebellion against the Tathāgata: he split the harmonious Saṃgha, shed the blood of the Buddha, and incited Ajātaśatru to murder his father, the king. Day after day he gathered abundant and delicious food and drink, yet out of arrogance he claimed to be equal to the Buddha, and for the sake of minor gains and offerings, he burned himself with fire.
"Even if all the Buddhas were to wish to rescue him, they would be unable to benefit him; it is like a mule that conceives a fetus, which will inevitably lead to its own death.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"As you have said, Devadatta has constantly harbored a heart of enmity and malice toward me. He has created for himself the causes and conditions for the Avīci Hell, such that no Buddhas can save or liberate him."
"I feel the utmost compassion for Devadatta, yet before long he shall be oppressed by the retribution of his own suffering karma.

When Devadatta was standing by the Buddha's side, he heard these words and became greatly incensed; he immediately left the Buddha and went with his disciples to the kingdom of Magadha to seek refuge with Ajātaśatru.
On the way, there were flocks of crows that cried out with urgent voices, fluttering and flitting about in agitation;
furthermore, they encountered a vicious bull that sought to gore them.
When the disciples saw these omens, they spoke to him, saying:
"We who now observe these various omens do not consider them auspicious; wherever we go, there will surely be no benefit.
Devadatta replied to them, saying, "You are all foolish; what do you know?"
"Just follow me quickly; there is no need for many words.
Having arrived in the kingdom of Magadha, he said to the gatekeeper:
"Enter and inform the king that I am here."
Then the gatekeeper entered and informed the king.
Upon hearing that Devadatta had arrived outside, King Ajātaśatru became greatly incensed and spoke these words:
"I do not wish even to hear his name; how much less should I ever behold him with my own eyes?"
For example, just as rain and hail strike down grasses and trees, which do not remain upon the ground for long but soon dissolve away of their own accord;
so too it is with such evil persons: they teach others to commit evil and destroy the roots of goodness in others, yet they themselves likewise ruin the seeds of their own roots of goodness.
The King commanded the gatekeepers not to allow him to proceed.
When Devadatta saw that King Ajātaśatru would not permit him to enter, his heart was filled with great anguish; he raised his hands to strike his head, gnashed his teeth, and uttered curses.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā was leaving the royal palace and, seeing Devadatta outside the gate, rebuked him, saying:
"Now the Śākya clan shall not flourish; you are creating a great obstacle within the Buddha-dharma."
When Devadatta heard these words, he became extremely incensed; he immediately struck her on the head with his rolled-up hand, and that bhikṣuṇī passed away instantly.
Furthermore, because Devadatta had harmed an arhat bhikṣuṇī, the earth immediately split open; a great, fierce fire enveloped his body and dragged him into hell.
At that time, having finished his bath, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus in verse:
"Just as when traveling a wicked path, One encounters long-lasting anxiety and fear;
But if one reaches level ground, There is peace and security, free from sorrow and affliction."
The perilous and narrow path of birth and death constantly terrifies sentient beings;
only the Way of Nirvāṇa allows the practitioner to attain peace and security.
I now desire to reach that place of eternal bliss and merit.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, went to Rājagṛha and extensively expounded the various Dharmas for the assembly of bhikṣus;
gradually proceeding to Pāṭaliputra, he extensively expounded the various Dharmas for the people, elders, householders, brahmins, and others;
and gradually arriving again at the city of Vaiśālī, he extensively proclaimed the various Dharmas for the Licchavis and the Licchavī women.
At that time, the World-Honored One was afflicted by illness throughout his entire body, and every part of him was in pain. He then looked toward Venerable Ānanda and said:
"At this moment, my body is entirely in pain; I wish only to cast off this decayed and worn-out body."
Ānanda, you should know that if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī attains the four bases of psychic power, they can remain in the world for a full kalpa, or for slightly less than a kalpa.
"How much more so, then, is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his desires?
At that time, Ānanda remained silent and gave no answer because he was obscured by Māra; even when asked a second and a third time, he remained silent.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"You should now go to the foot of a tree and, with focused diligence, contemplate and correctly observe all phenomena."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, I entreated the World-Honored One to enter parinirvāṇa; at that time, the World-Honored One replied to me, saying:
'Because my disciples—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—are not yet fully perfected, it is therefore not yet appropriate for me to enter parinirvāṇa.'"
“World-Honored One, now that the fourfold assembly is fully complete and those to be delivered have all been saved, we only pray that the Sugata will quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Māra:
“Excellent, Pāpīyān!”
"You should know that after three months, the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa.

When Māra Pāpīyān saw that the Buddha had granted his request, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his celestial palace.

At that time, having granted the celestial Māra’s request that he enter parinirvāṇa three months hence, the Tathāgata immediately relinquished his immeasurable lifespan and, through the power of his supernormal faculties, sustained his life for three months.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways; the sun lost its brilliance, and the wind and rain deviated from their natural course. The eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, were all struck with awe and terror, coming to the place where the Buddha was until they filled the air.
At that time, when the Venerable Ānanda saw this omen, his heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; he hurried to the Buddha's presence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what cause and condition has this omen suddenly appeared?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The evil Māra Pāpīyān has just come to my presence and entreated me to enter parinirvāṇa.
I have already granted him this request and have accordingly relinquished my life-span; however, by means of my supernormal power, I shall remain for three months."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“The World-Honored One has often taught that a person who possesses the four bases of spiritual power can, by the mastery of their own will, remain for a kalpa or for slightly less than a kalpa.”
"How is it that the Tathāgata will not remain long in the world, being subject to the same nature as all conditioned phenomena?
At that time, the Tathāgata replied to Ānanda:
"I have already spoken these words to you; because Māra obscured your mind, you did not know to request that I remain."
“I have already granted them [their request]; how then can I remain in this world?
Ānanda, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like this; they cannot endure forever.
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, Ānanda was overcome with confusion and distress, unable to restrain himself; he wailed and wept, deeply repenting and reproaching himself.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, traveled gradually through various kingdoms, villages, and settlements, extensively expounding the various Dharmas; those whom he converted and delivered were beyond calculation.
Gradually proceeding further, he arrived at the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Hiranyavatī River in the country of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, and said to Ānanda:
"Prepare a couch with its head toward the north; my body is now in extreme pain, and at midnight I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
Ānanda received the instruction and, having spread out the rope-couch, the Buddha immediately lay down upon it, resting on his right side.
At that time, having seen the Buddha lying down, Ānanda hid behind the Buddha and wept with streaming tears, overcome by extreme anguish and distress.
The World-Honored One then asked the bhikṣus:
"Where is Ānanda now? The bhikṣus replied:
Standing close behind the Buddha, he shed tears in grief and distress.
The Tathāgata then addressed Ānanda with a voice of great compassion and Brahma-like resonance, saying:
"You should not now weep like an infant."
Why is this so? Within the cycle of birth and death, all things are exactly like this; you should simply focus your mindfulness and contemplate all dharmas.
From the past until now, as you have attended upon me, your actions of body, speech, and mind have been exceedingly pure and wholesome; I have never seen even the slightest fault in you.
"Now you should diligently seek liberation; endure the severing of your compassionate heart and do not torment yourself.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, how should the method for his cremation be performed?"

The Buddha told Ānanda: "The method for cremation is like that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King: take one thousand pieces of fresh, pure cotton cloth to wrap the Buddha’s body; sprinkle fragrant oil over it and place it within a golden coffin; then place the golden coffin within a silver coffin; then place the silver coffin within a copper coffin; then place the copper coffin within an iron coffin; pile up various types of fragrant wood and perform the cremation; then collect the relics and erect stupas, masts, banners, canopies, and provide all manner of offerings."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Go now into the city and inform the Mallas, saying: 'I am here; I shall enter nirvāṇa tonight. If you wish to come, you should know for yourselves the proper time.'"
Ānanda, having received the command, immediately entered the city and proclaimed in a loud voice throughout the streets, alleys, and roads:
"The Great Teacher of the Three Realms—the Tathāgata, the Arhat—is now staying near the twin trees; he shall enter parinirvāṇa at midnight."
"If any of you wish to pay homage, make offerings, or seek clarification through inquiry,
you should know that now is the time. When the Mallas heard these words, they were all deeply distressed and asked Ānanda,
"How swiftly has the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa?"
"From this day forth, we shall have no one to rely upon.
Shedding tears as they went along the road, they proceeded to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the area surrounding the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River—extending four hundred and eighty li in circumference—was so densely packed with the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others that there was not a single empty space between them; all were filled with longing and affection, wailing in grief and suffering, and all spoke thus:
"The world has lost its compassionate father," they said to one another,
"From this day forward we shall sink into the cycle of birth and death; who will deliver us?"

At that time, there was in the city a brahmin named Subhadra, one hundred and twenty years of age. Hearing that the Buddha was nearby between the twin śāla trees and was about to enter parinirvāṇa at midnight, he went immediately to the Buddha’s location and said to Ānanda:
“I have heard that the Tathāgata—the All-Knowing One—is about to enter parinirvāṇa at midnight. I wish to resolve a few doubts; I only pray that you will allow me to approach.”
At that time, Ānanda thought to himself:
"This brahmin has long practiced heterodox views; he will surely engage in debate with the Buddha now, thereby causing disturbance to the World-Honored One who is suffering from physical pain."
He remained silent and did not grant permission, even when the request was made a second and a third time.
At that moment, the World-Honored One heard them from afar with his divine ear and said to Ānanda:
"You may allow this old brahmin to come forward; he shall be my very last disciple."
Having seen the Buddha, Subhadra was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated himself, touching his head to the ground in salutation.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught him the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path according to his capacity, and Subhadra immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship while still seated. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have already been graced by the opportunity to cross the bitter sea of birth and death. I cannot bear to witness the Great Teacher’s parinirvāṇa; I shall now enter extinction first."
He immediately entered parinirvāṇa before the Buddha.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had preached the sublime Dharma for the entire assembly of the eight classes of beings, when midnight arrived and the time for his nirvāṇa had come, he spoke these verses:
"For all sentient beings, The conditions for my deliverance are now complete."

"The night is still and the atmosphere is tranquil; the time for Nirvāṇa has arrived. Then, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One entered the first dhyāna. Having entered the first dhyāna, he further entered the second dhyāna;
